en: For washed burdock: bag it and refrigerate, per the same source. Cut surfaces brown within minutes, so drop pieces into water with a splash of vinegar.

There is no honest day count for burrata — go by the use-by date on the tub, which is short, and in the UK the Food Standards Agency's rule is that a use-by date is a legal limit, not a suggestion: eat, cook or freeze it by then. Keep it at 0–5 °C in its own liquid, and take it out only 20 minutes before serving. Once you cut the pouch the cream runs and the whole thing is a one-sitting food.
Do not freeze it. The point of burrata is a molten cream centre inside an elastic curd, and freezing destroys both.
May be left at room temperature for 1 - 2 days.

Wrap it in its own foil or in waxed paper and put it in a closed box — cabrales is aggressive and will perfume everything in the fridge, butter and eggs first. Keep it at or below 40 °F (4 °C). It goes on ripening: it darkens, softens and gets stronger and saltier. When it turns runny brown at the edges and smells of ammonia rather than of blue, it is finished.
Freeze it only for cooking — into a sauce for meat, which is what most of it gets used for anyway. It thaws crumbly and weeping.
Unopened, cool and dark. Commercial cajeta is heat-processed and very high in sugar; the date on the jar is the guide. The goat's milk gives it a tang that deepens with age, which is not spoilage.

Covered, at or below 40 °F (4 °C), clean spoon every time. Cajeta is looser and more pourable than most dulce de leche, so it is more likely to be contaminated by drips and double-dipping. Cajeta envinada carries a little alcohol, which helps it keep, but not enough to make it shelf-stable once opened.
Thin-skinned and small, so they dry out faster than a lime on the counter.
In a sealed bag or box in the crisper to hold the juice in.
Freeze the squeezed juice in an ice cube tray; the whole fruit turns to mush.
Extremely acidic and extremely soft; it is picked and pulped almost immediately in Amazonia and rarely reaches a market fresh.
Frozen pulp is the normal traded form.
Ripen at room temperature until the skin is deep orange and the fruit gives all over; unripe canistel is chalky and astringent.
Only once soft. The flesh is dry and dense like a boiled yolk and dries out further in cold air, so wrap it.
Freeze the mashed flesh.
Leave the papery husk on. CTAHR notes that removing the husk reduces postharvest life, so de-husk only what you are about to eat.
Husked fruit should be packed no deeper than a pint container and chilled as soon as possible.
Freeze husked fruit on a tray, then bag.

NMSU gives cooked meat and meat dishes 3 to 4 days at or below 40 °F (4 °C). Get it into shallow containers within 2 hours of coming out of the pot — a deep tub of hot pork in fat holds its heat for hours, which is exactly the wrong thing. Keeping the meat submerged in its own strained fat seals it from air and helps, but it is not a cure and does not extend the safe window.
Freeze in portions with a spoonful of the fat and a splash of the cooking juices, which is what stops it drying to string. Reheat spread out in a hot dry pan so it crisps, not in a microwave.
Does not need to be refrigerated.

USDA Agriculture Handbook 66: fresh cassava roots are highly perishable under ambient conditions and become unmarketable in 3 days or less. The failure is vascular streaking — blue-purple lines through the flesh, worst at the cut end and at any break in the skin. Cut a root across before cooking and discard it if it is streaked.

AH-66: cassava is chilling sensitive but tolerates 0 to 5 °C (32 to 41 °F) with minimal symptoms provided it is used as soon as it comes out of storage. Wax-coated import roots hold over 30 days at that temperature commercially; an unwaxed root in a home fridge loses water fast, so wrap it in plastic or a damp cloth and treat one to two weeks as the limit.
Peel, cut into chunks, remove the woody core and freeze raw, or boil first and freeze cooked. Do not freeze it in the skin.

Keep at 0 °F (−18 °C) in the unopened bag; reseal tightly once opened or the chunks frost-burn white and cook woolly. Cook from frozen — boil until a fork goes through with no resistance. Do not thaw and refreeze.

Once boiled, keep cooked cassava covered at 40 °F (4 °C) or below and use within 3 to 4 days, the general NMSU figure for a cooked dish. It sets hard and starchy in the fridge; reheat it in its cooking liquid, or fry it.

A whole, properly dried Spanish cecina hangs in a cool, dry, airy place like a dry-cured ham does. The salt and the water loss are the preservation. Wrap the cut face in a cloth, not plastic. This applies to a hard, fully cured piece — not to the moist Mexican cecina below.

Once vacuum-packed slices are opened, or a piece is cut into, refrigerate at or below 40 °F (4 °C) and use within two to three weeks. Mexican cecina — thin sheets of beef salted only briefly, often sold red with chile as cecina enchilada — is a fresh product, not a cured one: keep it refrigerated and cook it within 2 to 3 days, or freeze it.
Freezing a dry cure is about stopping the fat oxidising rather than about safety. Interleave the slices with paper. Long freezing makes cured beef dull and tallowy.
Strongly aromatic once ripe; keep it out of a closed room.
Separate the pulp segments and seal them in an airtight box so the smell does not transfer.
Freeze the segments; they are usually battered and fried straight from frozen.

Taiwan's 農業部 says finished century eggs should be kept somewhere cool and well ventilated, in the shell, and used by the printed date. The alkaline cure raises the pH to roughly 9–12, which is what preserves them; do not treat a cracked, weeping or ammonia-reeking egg as merely old.

農業部 warns that refrigerated century eggs sweat when they come back up to room temperature, and condensation on a porous shell invites contamination — so if you do refrigerate them, take out only what you will eat.
Once peeled, a century egg is an unprotected ready-to-eat food: cover it and keep it at 4 °C or below.

Make it and eat it the same day, kept covered at or below 40 °F (4 °C) and never left out for more than 2 hours — the FDA's limit for seafood, one hour above 90 °F. It is at its best within the hour anyway; the acid keeps working and the fish goes chalky and dry overnight. Marinate in the fridge, not on the counter.
Never freeze finished ceviche — the acid-firmed flesh thaws to cotton wool. Freezing belongs at the other end: freeze the fish before you make the dish, to kill parasites.

Stack them hot in a cloth-lined casserole so the steam keeps them pliable, and eat them the day they are made. There is no fat and no preservative in a plain chapati, so by day two they are leathery and by day three they mould, faster in a humid kitchen.
Wrap the cooled stack airtight — refrigeration stales bread faster than the counter does, but it is what holds off mould. Bring them back with fifteen seconds on a dry hot tawa, not the microwave.
Interleave with baking paper and freeze flat; griddle from frozen.

A cool room suits chayote better than a cold fridge: Texas A&M gives ideal storage as 50 to 59 °F (10 to 15 °C) at 90 % humidity. The failure at room temperature is shrivelling and, eventually, a seedling pushing out of the broad end — a sprouted fruit is past eating, though it will grow into a vine.

University of Hawai'i CTAHR: chayote transports well for up to 6 weeks at 50 °F (10 °C) and 90 % relative humidity. Texas A&M puts chilling injury below 50 °F, which is colder than most domestic fridges run, so use the warmest drawer and expect pitting if it sits at the back. Both sources agree on the real enemy — chayotes shrivel badly under dry conditions regardless of temperature — so keep them in a loosely closed or perforated bag.
Peel, seed, dice and blanch before freezing; raw frozen chayote thaws to water. Frozen chayote is for soups and stews, never for a salad.

Sealed and dry, somewhere cool and dark. A puffed chicharrón is almost all rendered protein and fat with the water driven out, so it fails by going soft and then rancid rather than by growing anything. Once the bag is open it goes limp within a week or two in humid weather — clip the bag, or decant into a tin.

Do not refrigerate the dry puffed kind — it pulls moisture and turns leathery. The fridge is only for the wet styles: chicharrón prensado, chicharrón en salsa verde, or a meaty chicharrón still soft with fat. Those are cooked meat and keep 3 to 4 days at or below 40 °F (4 °C).
Unopened, use the printed date; the MHLW standard for 魚肉ねり製品 sets chilled storage at 10 °C or below for products that have not been retorted or made acidic or dry enough to be exempt.
The grilled skin is not a barrier. Wrap and refrigerate at 4 °C or below once the pack is opened.
Freezes better than kamaboko because it is usually cooked into soups and simmers afterwards, where the coarser thawed texture does not matter. Slice before freezing.

Unopened commercial jars keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard. The solids in a commercial jar — chilli flakes, fried soybeans, fried onion and garlic, sesame — have been fried until dry, which is why the jar is shelf-stable.

Ohio State Extension gives opened salad oils 1 to 3 months; that is the practical limit on an opened jar of commercial chilli crisp too, since the failure mode is the oil and the fried solids going rancid and stale rather than anything growing. Keep the solids under the oil.

Homemade chilli crisp that still contains soft, moist garlic, shallot or ginger has not been dried by the frying and is fresh low-acid produce under oil. Treat it exactly as NCHFP treats garlic in oil: refrigerate at 4 °C (40 °F) or lower and use within no more than 4 days, or freeze it.
NCHFP allows garlic in oil to be frozen 'for up to several months'. Freezing dulls the crunch but is the honest way to keep a homemade batch.

This is the one entry in the batch where the difference between two similar-looking jars is a safety difference. Chilli oil made by pouring hot oil over dried chilli flakes and dried spices, then strained or left with only dried solids, is low-risk and is what commercial jars are. Chilli oil holding fresh garlic, fresh ginger, fresh chilli, shallot or fresh herbs is low-acid produce sealed under oil in an oxygen-free environment — the classic setting for Clostridium botulinum. Ohioline's botulism factsheet states that spores on herbs, garlic or tomatoes placed in oil can produce toxin in the anaerobic mixture of flavoured oils, and that using dried rather than fresh aromatics reduces the risk. Never leave an oil holding fresh produce at room temperature.

For dried-aromatics and commercial chilli oil, the limit is the oil going rancid rather than anything microbial. Ohio State Extension's pantry chart gives opened salad oils 1 to 3 months. Keep the bottle capped, dark and away from the cooker; refrigeration extends it further at the cost of the oil clouding.

Any chilli oil containing fresh garlic, ginger, chilli, shallot or herbs. NCHFP's rule for garlic in oil is: make it fresh, store it in the refrigerator at 4 °C (40 °F) or lower, and use it within no more than 4 days. Ohioline puts it as 'refrigerate flavored oils and make an amount... that will be used in a few days'.

The safe way to keep a fresh-aromatic chilli oil for longer. NCHFP: garlic in oil 'may be frozen for long term storage for up to several months'. Freeze in a small jar with ½-inch headspace, or in an ice-cube tray.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture: do not let it dry out — put it in a plastic bag and keep it at room temperature, out of wind and direct sun. A whole unbroken tuber is the one that keeps.
Only for a cut piece: wrap the cut face tightly in cling film. The exposed flesh oxidises brown and turns slimy.
MAFF's guide to freezing vegetables at home gives about 3 weeks. Grate it, bag it flat and freeze; grated yam is used straight from frozen.

Ohio State Extension gives unopened vinegar 2 years. Chinkiang vinegar is a genuine aged vinegar brewed from glutinous rice and wheat bran — age is a selling point, and a bottle kept past its date is a quality question, not a safety one.
Ohioline gives opened vinegar 12 months. Cap it tightly and keep it dark; the malty top notes are the first thing to go. Sediment in the bottom of an aged bottle is normal.
Buy stems with tight closed buds; once the white flowers open the stems have gone woody. Bag them dry in the crisper.
For best quality, do not refrigerate or microwave.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture recommends misting the whole plant, bagging it and standing it root-end down in the fridge. Yellowing flowers are the first sign it is going.

This is a raw, high-moisture food — blended leaves, raw chilli, sometimes raw onion or garlic — with none of the salt, acid or cooking that preserves a jarred chutney. Refrigerate it the moment it is made, in a full container with as little air as possible. Coconut chutney is the short one: fresh grated coconut sours within a day even cold, and a chutney that has turned fizzy or smells yeasty is fermenting. Extra lime juice both keeps the green colour and helps it last.
Herb chutneys freeze well in ice-cube trays and thaw in minutes; coconut chutney does not — it separates into oil and grit. No source gives a limit, so treat a few months as the ceiling.

Unopened, to the use-by date on the pot, at 0–5 °C. FSA's rule is that a use-by date is the limit, not a suggestion, and that you can freeze right up to midnight on it. Clotted cream is made by holding cream at around 80 °C for hours until a crust forms, which is a heat treatment as well as a texture — but the pot is then filled and sealed cold, so the date is the date.

New Mexico State gives opened cream 3 to 4 days, and clotted cream is a cream, whatever the spoon says. Keep the crust intact and scoop from one side; the golden crust is a physical barrier and breaking it up across the whole surface exposes far more of the soft cream underneath.

It freezes better than pouring cream because there is so little water in it — at around 55 to 64 % fat, there is not much left to form ice crystals. Thaw it slowly in the fridge and stir the crust back in.

Freshly pressed coconut cream is a raw, unpasteurised, low-acid emulsion — closer to raw milk than to the tin. Get it to 4 °C or below straight from the press and use it within a day or two. It separates into a thick cap and thin liquid in the fridge; that is normal, stir it back. Sourness, fizzing or a sharp yeasty smell means it has gone.
Freeze in an ice-cube tray or a flat bag. The emulsion breaks on thawing and looks curdled — whisk or blend it back together, and use it in cooked dishes rather than for a raw dressing.
Store in an airtight container.
Refrigeration not recommended - makes it difficult to use.
Freezing not recommended - makes it difficult to use.
Applies to unopened coconut.
Critical to be stored in an airtight container.
Do not return to freezer once taken out.
Store in a dry, cool environment

Ohio State gives unopened hard cheese 4 to 6 months refrigerated. A vacuum-packed piece of Comté genuinely does this: it is a cooked, pressed, long-aged cheese with a low moisture content, which is precisely why it was invented — a wheel was a way to keep a summer's milk through an alpine winter.

Ohio State's figure for opened hard cheese. Wrap it in waxed or greaseproof paper, not clingfilm, and change the paper every few days; a cut face left airtight against plastic sweats and grows moulds much faster than one allowed to breathe in a box. The white crystalline crunch in a well-aged piece is tyrosine, not spoilage.
Possible but pointless for a cheese this good — freezing makes it crumbly. Grate it first if you are going to.

A big pot of congee left to cool slowly on the stove is a classic Bacillus cereus incubator — it is starchy, wet and cools from the outside in, so the middle stays warm for hours. Decant into shallow containers and refrigerate; do not leave the pot out overnight.

TFDA allows cooked starchy food two days at most at 5 °C or below, and anything longer must be frozen. Reheat to a rolling boil, not just warm — though note that boiling kills the bacteria and not the emetic toxin they may already have made.
Freezes well in single portions; the texture thins on thawing, so reheat and reduce.

This is the single most common Bacillus cereus vehicle. Spores survive the steamer, and a bowl of oily sticky rice cooling slowly on the counter is exactly the 25-30 °C window in which the emetic toxin forms — a toxin that reheating will not destroy. TFDA and MAFF both say cooked rice dishes must go above 60 °C or into the fridge, not sit out.
Spread it out in a shallow container so it chills fast rather than sitting warm in a deep pot, and get it to 5 °C or below. TFDA allows two days at most in the fridge; beyond that it must be frozen.
Portion while still warm-ish, wrap tightly, freeze quickly. Steam or microwave from frozen — the texture survives freezing far better than refrigeration.

Cooked pearls sitting in warm syrup on a counter are a wet cooked starch — the same Bacillus cereus risk as cooked rice, and the emetic toxin they can produce is not destroyed by reheating. Shops keep a batch for a few hours at most for texture reasons; that is not a food-safety allowance for a home pot left out all afternoon.
TFDA caps refrigerated storage of cooked starchy food at about two days at 5 °C or below. Be aware that the pearls go hard and cloudy in the fridge within hours — cook what you will drink.

Cooking sake sold as 料理酒 usually has salt added — the Tokyo Regional Taxation Bureau describes it as a fermented seasoning to which salt is added, which is what keeps it outside the liquor-tax system and off the licensed shelf. Alcohol plus salt makes it self-preserving: a cool dark cupboard, tightly capped, away from the cooker. Unsalted 料理清酒 is simply drinking sake and is treated the same way, though it oxidises faster and is worth refrigerating for flavour. No agency publishes a home shelf life, so none is given here.

A whole, uncut, fully cured coppa in its casing can hang in a cool, dry, airy larder at 12–16 °C like any dry-cured whole muscle, and will keep hardening. Once you cut into it, cover the face with a little of its own fat or a cloth and move it to the refrigerator — an opened cut surface on a piece this fatty oxidises quickly at room temperature.

A whole piece, or an unopened vacuum pack, wrapped in paper at or below 4 °C. Coppa is dry-cured pork neck — the fat is intramuscular and abundant, which is what makes it taste good and what eventually makes it go rancid rather than mouldy.

Sliced coppa is on the same clock as any sliced cured meat: a few days, tightly re-wrapped, at or below 4 °C. Whole and sliced are deliberately not given one number here. If the slices have gone dull brown at the edges and smell of old fat, that is rancidity, and no amount of refrigeration reverses it.
Keep tightly covered; refrigerate to extend storage life.

A properly aged cotija is dry, hard and heavily salted, and it keeps like a parmesan. Wrap it in waxed or greaseproof paper inside a loose bag — sealed plastic makes it sweat — and keep it at or below 40 °F (4 °C). NMSU gives unopened hard cheese 3 to 6 months and opened hard cheese about a month; a wedge already cut into is nearer the latter. Surface mould on a hard cheese can be cut a good inch away and the rest used.
Freezing a hard cheese makes it crumbly, which barely matters for something you were going to grate anyway. Freeze it in a block, not grated, and grate from part-frozen.

Couscous is not a grain — it is tiny pasta, rolled from semolina — so it stores like dry pasta: sealed, cool, dark, effectively indefinite in safety terms and limited by staling and insects. Wholemeal couscous carries the germ and should be treated like atta instead, at well under a year.
Cooked and cooled couscous, in a sealed container. Fluff it and cool it fast rather than leaving the bowl covered on the counter.
Use for cooking.

At or below 40 °F (4 °C), lid on, and never returned to the tub from a plate. Crema is cultured, so it sours further rather than going off cleanly — thin, separated whey on top can be stirred back in, but a fizzy, yeasty or bitter taste means it is finished. Squeeze bottles are worse than tubs for keeping it clean: wipe the nozzle.
Do not freeze it. Cultured cream splits into grains and water on thawing and will not come back, even stirred.

Ohio State Extension gives commercial sour cream two weeks refrigerated, and crème fraîche is the same thing at a higher fat content and a slightly milder acidity. Keep it at 0–5 °C. It thickens and sharpens as it sits; a little clear whey on top is normal and can be stirred back in.

Once the pot is open, always use a clean spoon — crème fraîche is far less acidic than yoghurt and a mould spore or a buttery knife will start a colony. Pink, grey or fuzzy growth means the whole pot goes; Hong Kong's CFS is blunt that mould hyphae run deeper than the visible patch and that you cannot scoop the toxin out.
Freezing splits it. The high fat means it survives better than sour cream and can be whisked back together for a sauce, but it will never be a spoonable garnish again. Better to buy small pots.

A croissant is crisp for about four hours and then it is a soft pastry, which is a different and lesser thing. Leave them uncovered on a rack for the first day — covering them traps the steam that is coming out of the laminated layers and turns the shell chewy. From day two they want three or four minutes in a 180 °C oven to drive the moisture back out; that works twice at most.

Pointless. The butter in the layers sets hard, the crumb stales faster, and you have to warm it anyway. Refrigerate only a croissant that has been filled with something perishable — ham, egg, crème pâtissière — in which case the filling sets the timeline, not the pastry, and that is a two-day food at or below 4 °C.

Freeze baked croissants the day they are made, in a sealed bag, and reheat from frozen at 180 °C for about 8 minutes — they come back closer to fresh than anything you can do on day three. Raw frozen croissant dough is a different product and follows its pack instructions.

This applies both to the chilled béchamel before shaping and to fried croquetas afterwards. The filling is a milk-and-flour paste enriched with cooked ham, chicken or fish — a wet, low-acid, ready-to-eat mixture that is handled a great deal by hand while being rolled and crumbed, which is exactly the profile that gets contaminated after cooking. Chill the béchamel spread thin in a tray, not deep in a bowl, cover it, and keep everything at or below 40 °F (4 °C).

Freezing is the right way to keep croquetas, and it should happen at the raw, crumbed stage. Freeze them apart on a tray, then bag. Fry them from frozen in properly hot oil — a thawed croqueta bursts. Refried, previously frozen croquetas are not worth eating.

In their bag, at room temperature, or to the printed date on a supermarket pack. Crumpets are wetter than any bread here — they are a pourable batter, cooked on one side only, and the famous holes run right through an open, humid crumb. That makes them a fast mould substrate, and a bag of crumpets in a warm kitchen will show blue-green spots inside a few days.

This is the one bread product where the fridge is genuinely the right answer, and it is worth understanding why. Refrigeration's penalty is accelerated staling — but you are going to toast a crumpet anyway, and toasting reverses staling by re-gelatinising the starch. So you pay nothing and you buy real time against mould: the bread study cited found no visible mould at all over 10 days at 8.2 °C. New Mexico State gives shop-bought bread and baked goods 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated.
Freeze them interleaved and toast from frozen on a slightly longer setting. No thawing needed and no quality loss worth mentioning.

A butter dish on the counter is fine for a day or two, and no longer for an unsalted cultured butter — this is the style most likely to go rancid on you, because the culture leaves it slightly acidic and it usually carries little or no salt. Keep the dish covered and out of the light; light and air, not bacteria, are what turn butter.

New Mexico State gives butter 1 to 2 months refrigerated. Keep it wrapped and in the door-free part of the fridge if you can; Ohio State takes the stricter line of 1 to 2 weeks, and that is the better guide for quality, because butter picks up every smell in the fridge and cultured butter has a delicate flavour to lose.
New Mexico State gives 6 to 9 months. Freeze it in its original wrapper inside a bag; the wrapper is greaseproof and the bag keeps the smells out. Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter.
The thick brown rind protects the pulp; the fruit is normally opened as soon as it drops.
Scoop the pulp off the seeds and keep it covered.
Frozen pulp is the standard form outside Brazil.

Set it at room temperature only until it firms, then get it straight into the fridge — the culture keeps working in the cold, just slowly, so a batch that is pleasant on day two is sharply sour by day five. Never dip a used spoon into the pot; that is what makes a batch go slimy or pink.
